1) Clearly pointing out the goals of a specific concept instead of just writing a definition, relevant proposition, or theorem, and then moving on to corollaries.  Many instructors in the past, under the flag of "it should be obvious" have left behind important notions to understand why a certain approach is taken for a proof, but in this course, the instructor was especially rigorous with constant call-back to what concepts apply from prior topics to come up with a trick or pattern to understand and replicate a proof.
2) Additional assistance outside of class is very rarely useful from instructors as far as I have experienced. There are a handful of instructors in the department that have adequately responded to my emails, regardless of urgency, and in this course, the instructor always made sure to answer and help throughout the entirety of the semester, regardless of how possibly mundane my questions or answers to questions may have been.
3) Additionally, the teacher never skipped a class or left a topic to be studied by students. In my experience, many instructors have left examples on the students instead of being involved with helping understand some principle examples. In this course, the instructor neither skipped classes, nor ever left anything important as a part of something we should learn on our own.

instructor:
Probably the best instructor in the department. Prior to every novel topic, he provides the students with complete, alluring motivation to proceed. He clearly states what is expected from the student, from the proofs to the exams. He practices the main rule of lecturing; first, explain what you will tell, then tell it, lastly, repeat what you have told. His attitude towards mathematics is that it should be practiced rigorously, while retaining the essential ideas. This really makes the classes different from just-copy-from-the-book-lectures by other instructors in the department. He also occasionally references some further advanced topics, not too much and not too rare, it makes the topic tenfold more enjoyable. I congratulate him for sustaining this balance for an advanced mathematics course like PDE.

A rather weak point is that sometimes, necessarily, there are long & laborious proofs; I know it is better to explain them step-by-step yet sometimes the proof gets over-complicated or full on stops due to a confusion. These are minor occurrences but they heavily disengage you from you are being actively listening at that moment.

He made the course hard. At some times, the lectures were very hard to follow. They felt like seminars. There should have been weekly homework instead of quizzes. He posted some suggested exercises from the book, but there were a lot of questions to solve realistically. The book does not have a solution manual either, which makes everything harder when I am supposed to make perfectly rigorous proofs in the exams. If your major is anything but mathematics, do not take this course. Despite having pre's that are not strictly for mathematics students, it is clearly not designed for non-majors in mind. The course is not really helpful in understanding and solving PDE's. The exams are really hard, not because of the number of questions but because it is not possible to finish four questions (each having three sub-questions) within a time of 90 minutes. However, he keeps saying these questions are trivial, so they should have been finished by this time very easily. I just learned this stuff a few weeks ago, and it is not trivial for me.

The course itself was very difficult to manage in terms of content, but the instructor made the assessments reasonably easy to follow along with, providing ample practice problems and supplementary handouts. No real weaknesses for the instructor, by far the best instructor in the Mathematics Department.
